\chapter{Greetings}
\label{ch:greetings}
\hlchaptermodality{1}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can greet someone in Kannada, recognize the reply, and choose an appropriate response.}

Read all five words straight off the page, then say which two are Sanskrit loans and which three are native Dravidian.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[namaskāra]{\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ} (namaskāra) — \textquotedblleft{}greetings,\textquotedblright{} a making of a bow}

\label{lesson:KA-C01-namaskara}



\begin{quote}
Meet your first Kannada word. Say \textbf{namaskāra} with a small bow: “hello” or “greetings.” Now read it one small piece at a time.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Kannada runs \textbf{left to right}. A consonant normally carries a built-in \textbf{a}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನ} · \kn{ಮ} · \kn{ರ}} = \emph{na · ma · ra}.
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಕಾ}} = \textbf{\kn{ಕ}} \emph{ka} plus the long-\emph{ā} vowel sign: \emph{kā}.
  \item In \textbf{\kn{ಸ್ಕ}}, \textbf{\kn{ಸ}} loses its vowel and stacks with \textbf{\kn{ಕ}}: \emph{s + ka = ska}.
\end{itemize}

Left to right: \textbf{\kn{ನ} · \kn{ಮ} · \kn{ಸ್} · \kn{ಕಾ} · \kn{ರ}} = \emph{na-ma-s-kā-ra} $\to$

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}} = \textbf{namaskāra}
\end{quote}

You just read Kannada.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}} came from Sanskrit \textbf{namas} (“a bow”) + \textbf{kāra} (“a making,” from \emph{kṛ}, “to do”): literally \textbf{“the making of a bow.”} Kannada borrowed the whole word. Tamil instead kept its native greeting, \emph{vaṇakkam}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=violet!6,colframe=violet!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Across the family — the same idea, five ways}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Hello\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{Source} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Kannada} & \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ} \emph{namaskāra} & Sanskrit \\
Telugu & \emph{namaskāram} & Sanskrit \\
Malayalam & \emph{namaskāram} & Sanskrit \\
Hindi & \emph{namaste} & Sanskrit \\
Tamil & \emph{vaṇakkam} & \textbf{native Dravidian} \\
English & \emph{hello} & Germanic \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Tamil alone kept its own word; the rest lean on the Sanskrit \emph{namas-}.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{culture}
With palms together and a small bow, \emph{namaskāra} works as \textbf{hello or goodbye}. It is respectful without being stiff.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} read it left to right — na · ma · s · kā · ra $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}namaskāra\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} what happens to \kn{ಸ} in \kn{ಸ್ಕ} (loses its vowel, stacks under ka)
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}namaskāra,\textquotedblright{} with a small bow — you are offering respect
  \item \emph{Write it:} trace \textbf{\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}} with a finger, then copy it once
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}}. What does it mean? (“Greetings.”) What does it literally mean? (Sanskrit \emph{namas} + \emph{kāra}: “the making of a bow.”)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dhanyavāda]{\kn{ಧನ್ಯವಾದ} (dhanyavāda) — \textquotedblleft{}thank you,\textquotedblright{} an utterance of \textquotedblleft{}worthy\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:KA-C01-dhanyavada}



\begin{quote}
The word for gratitude — and another Sanskrit loan, so a chance to see the \emph{same} borrowed word Kannada shares with Telugu and Hindi.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Kannada.)}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಧ}} = \textquotedblleft{}dha\textquotedblright{} — an \textbf{aspirated} \emph{d} (a real puff of breath after it).
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನ್ಯ}} = \textquotedblleft{}nya\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\kn{ನ}} (na) loses its vowel and stacks with \textbf{\kn{ಯ}} (ya) as a conjunct (the same stacking you saw in \emph{namaskāra}).
  \item \textbf{\kn{ವಾ}} = \textquotedblleft{}vā\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\kn{ವ}} (va) with the \textquotedblleft{}ā\textquotedblright{} vowel sign.
  \item \textbf{\kn{ದ}} = \textquotedblleft{}da.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

Left to right: \textbf{\kn{ಧ} · \kn{ನ್ಯ} · \kn{ವಾ} · \kn{ದ}} = \emph{dha-nya-vā-da} $\to$

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಧನ್ಯವಾದ}} = \textbf{dhanyavāda}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಧನ್ಯವಾದ}} (\emph{dhanyavāda}) is \textbf{Sanskrit}: \textbf{dhanya} (\textquotedblleft{}worthy, blessed,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{dhana}, \textquotedblleft{}wealth\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{vāda} (\textquotedblleft{}a saying, an utterance,\textquotedblright{} from the root \emph{vad}, \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}). Literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}an utterance of '{[}you are{]} worthy'\textquotedblright{}} — a formal, dignified thanks. It is the \textbf{same word} as Hindi \emph{dhanyavād} and Telugu \emph{dhanyavādamulu}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=violet!6,colframe=violet!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Across the family — the same idea, five ways}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Thanks\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{Note} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Kannada} & \emph{dhanyavāda} (\kn{ಧನ್ಯವಾದ}) & \textbf{Sanskrit} (\emph{dhanya} + \emph{vāda}) \\
Telugu & \emph{dhanyavādamulu} (\te{ధన్యవాదములు}) & Sanskrit — same word \\
Hindi & \emph{dhanyavād} (\dv{धन्यवाद}) & Sanskrit — same word \\
Tamil & \emph{naṉṟi} (\ta{நன்றி}) & \textbf{native} (\textquotedblleft{}goodness\textquotedblright{}) \\
Malayalam & \emph{nandi} (\ml{നന്ദി}) & \textbf{native} — Tamil's cousin \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Here the split is stark: Kannada, Telugu, and Hindi all use the Sanskrit \emph{dhanyavāda}, while Tamil and Malayalam keep the native Dravidian \emph{naṉṟi / nandi}. Kannada sits on the Sanskrit-borrowing side of its own family.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{culture}
\emph{dhanyavāda} is the formal, written \textquotedblleft{}thank you.\textquotedblright{} In warm everyday Kannada people often reach for the English \emph{thanks}, or simply show gratitude in tone and gesture; the full \emph{dhanyavāda} carries weight, for when you mean to mark it.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item dha · nya · vā · da $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}dhanyavāda\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two Sanskrit blocks — \emph{dhanya} (\textquotedblleft{}worthy\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{vāda} (\textquotedblleft{}a saying\textquotedblright{})
  \item notice \kn{ಧ} is \emph{dha}, a breathy \emph{d} — not a plain \emph{d}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\kn{ಧನ್ಯವಾದ}}. What are its two Sanskrit pieces? (\emph{dhanya} \textquotedblleft{}worthy\textquotedblright{} + \emph{vāda} \textquotedblleft{}a saying.\textquotedblright{}) Which two Dravidian languages use a \emph{native} word for thanks instead? (Tamil \emph{naṉṟi}, Malayalam \emph{nandi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[haudu]{\kn{ಹೌದು} (haudu) — \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:KA-C01-haudu}



\begin{quote}
After two Sanskrit loans, a \textbf{native Kannada} word — the plain \textquotedblleft{}yes.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Kannada.)}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಹೌ}} = \textquotedblleft{}hau\textquotedblright{} — the consonant \textbf{\kn{ಹ}} (ha) carrying the \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}au\textquotedblright{} vowel sign} (the two little marks that hug the letter).
  \item \textbf{\kn{ದು}} = \textquotedblleft{}du\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\kn{ದ}} (da) with the \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}u\textquotedblright{} vowel sign} hooked beneath.
\end{itemize}

Left to right: \textbf{\kn{ಹೌ} · \kn{ದು}} = \emph{hau-du} $\to$

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಹೌದು}} = \textbf{haudu} = \textquotedblleft{}yes.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಹೌದು}} (\emph{haudu}) is the everyday \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}yes / that's so,\textquotedblright{}} a genuinely native Kannada word (not a Sanskrit loan). Its polite-agreement cousins — \emph{audu}, \emph{houdu} in speech — all circle the same \textquotedblleft{}it is so.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Dravidian often answers by echoing the verb}]
Like its sister Tamil, Kannada frequently answers \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{} by \textbf{repeating the verb} rather than using a stand-alone word: asked \emph{\textquotedblleft{}bandiddīyā?\textquotedblright{}} (\textquotedblleft{}have you come?\textquotedblright{}), a natural yes is \emph{\textquotedblleft{}bandiddēne\textquotedblright{}} (\textquotedblleft{}I have come\textquotedblright{}). Keep \emph{haudu} as the simple all-purpose \textquotedblleft{}yes,\textquotedblright{} but expect a \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{} to come back as a whole verb — a habit shared right across the Dravidian family.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hau · du $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}haudu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the \textquotedblleft{}au\textquotedblright{} vowel sign on \kn{ಹ}, then the \textquotedblleft{}u\textquotedblright{} sign under \kn{ದ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}haudu\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}yes, that's so\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\kn{ಹೌದು}}. Is it native Kannada or a Sanskrit loan? (Native.) Besides \emph{haudu}, how else might a Kannada speaker say \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}? (By echoing the question's verb — e.g. \emph{bandiddēne}, \textquotedblleft{}I have come.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[illa]{\kn{ಇಲ್ಲ} (illa) — \textquotedblleft{}no,\textquotedblright{} and a word Tamil shares almost exactly}

\label{lesson:KA-C01-illa}



\begin{quote}
The partner of \emph{haudu} — and a beautiful piece of family evidence: this Kannada \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} is essentially the \textbf{same word} as Tamil's \emph{illai}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Kannada.)}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಇ}} = \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}i\textquotedblright{}} — an \textbf{independent vowel} (the word starts with it, so it gets a full letter, not a hooked-on sign).
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಲ್ಲ}} = \textquotedblleft{}lla\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\kn{ಲ}} (la) loses its vowel and stacks under another \textbf{\kn{ಲ}} (la): a doubled, held \textquotedblleft{}ll.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

Left to right: \textbf{\kn{ಇ} · \kn{ಲ್ಲ}} = \emph{i-lla} $\to$

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}} = \textbf{illa}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{illa}) is built on the old Dravidian root \textbf{il}, \textquotedblleft{}not-being, absence\textquotedblright{} — so, like Tamil \emph{illai}, it is really the statement \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}{[}it{]} is not, {[}there{]} is not,\textquotedblright{}} doing duty as the everyday \textquotedblleft{}no.\textquotedblright{} Its positive twin is \textbf{\kn{ಇದೆ}} (\emph{ide}), \textquotedblleft{}there is.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Dravidian negates by \emph{being}, not with a \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{}-word}]
English inserts \emph{not} / \emph{no} to make a sentence negative. Kannada — exactly like Tamil — instead swaps in the \textbf{negative verb of existence}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pustaka \textbf{ide}} — \textquotedblleft{}there \textbf{is} a book.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{pustaka \textbf{illa}} — \textquotedblleft{}there \textbf{is not} a book.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

So \emph{illa} is both the plain \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} and the word that negates a whole sentence. This is a \textbf{shared Dravidian inheritance}: Tamil \emph{illai}, Kannada \emph{illa}, Malayalam \emph{illa} — one family, one way of saying a thing is not.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=violet!6,colframe=violet!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Across the family — the same idea, five ways}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}No / isn't\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{Note} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Kannada} & \emph{illa} (\kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}) & native Dravidian (root \emph{il}) \\
Tamil & \emph{illai} (\ta{இல்லை}) & the \textbf{same} root \\
Malayalam & \emph{illa} (\ml{ഇല്ല}) & the \textbf{same} root \\
Telugu & \emph{lēdu} (\te{లేదు}) & native Dravidian, a different root \\
Hindi & \emph{nahīṁ} (\dv{नहीं}) & Indo-European \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three of the four Dravidian languages share \emph{il-}; only Telugu picked a different native root. Hindi, from the other family entirely, is unrelated.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item i · lla $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}illa\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \emph{haudu} (\textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}) / \emph{illa} (\textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pustaka illa\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}there is no book\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}}. Literally, is it closer to \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}is not\textquotedblright{}? (\textquotedblleft{}Is not / there is not.\textquotedblright{}) Which two other Dravidian languages share this exact root? (Tamil \emph{illai}, Malayalam \emph{illa}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sari]{\kn{ಸರಿ} (sari) — \textquotedblleft{}okay,\textquotedblright{} the word that oils every conversation}

\label{lesson:KA-C01-sari}



\begin{quote}
The easy middle between \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}: \textquotedblleft{}okay, alright, fine, correct.\textquotedblright{} And Tamil has the very same word — the Dravidian family shares it whole.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Kannada.)}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಸ}} = \textquotedblleft{}sa.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\kn{ರಿ}} = \textquotedblleft{}ri\textquotedblright{} — the consonant \textbf{\kn{ರ}} (ra) with the \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}i\textquotedblright{} vowel sign}.
\end{itemize}

Left to right: \textbf{\kn{ಸ} · \kn{ರಿ}} = \emph{sa-ri} $\to$

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಸರಿ}} = \textbf{sari} = \textquotedblleft{}okay / correct.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Two clean syllables — no conjunct, no stacking — a good moment to feel how smoothly Kannada's round letters read.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಸರಿ}} (\emph{sari}) is native Dravidian for \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}correct, even, right,\textquotedblright{}} and by an easy step, \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}okay, agreed.\textquotedblright{}} It is the verbal nod of Kannada, just as it is of Tamil (\textbf{\ta{சரி}}, \emph{sari}) — the \textbf{same word} across the family. Doubled, \emph{sari sari}, it means \textquotedblleft{}yes, yes, alright.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one shared Dravidian word, two scripts}]
\emph{sari} is a small proof of how close these languages are: identical word, identical meaning, written in two different scripts — Kannada \textbf{\kn{ಸರಿ}}, Tamil \textbf{\ta{சரி}}. As you learn to read each script, watching a shared word change its clothes but not its sound is the fastest way to feel the family resemblance. (This \textquotedblleft{}same word, different script\textquotedblright{} pattern-matching is exactly what carries you across Kannada, Telugu, and Malayalam.)
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item sa · ri $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}sari\textquotedblright{}
  \item the everyday triple — \emph{haudu} (yes) · \emph{illa} (no) · \emph{sari} (okay)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sari, sari\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}alright, alright\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\kn{ಸರಿ}}. What does it literally mean, and what does it do in conversation? (\textquotedblleft{}Correct/even\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}okay, agreed.\textquotedblright{}) Is it native or borrowed, and which sister language spells the same word \textbf{\ta{சரி}}? (Native Dravidian; Tamil.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[na]{\kn{ನ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S01-letter-na}



\begin{quote}
Rounded and looping like Telugu (its sister script), most letters topped by a small curved headstroke; no continuous top line.

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ನ}}
\textbf{\kn{ನ}} — \emph{na}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{n}, it is \textbf{na}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{ನ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}} \emph{namaskāra} — hello / greetings (namaskāra — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಧನ್ಯವಾದ}} \emph{dhanyavāda} — thank you (dhanyavāda — \textquotedblleft{}an utterance of 'worthy'\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ನ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{ನ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{ನ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}  ·  \kn{ಧನ್ಯವಾದ}  ·  \kn{ಹೌದು}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ನ} three times, saying \emph{na} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{ನ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ನ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{na}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 1 — a five-word recap}

\label{lesson:KA-C01-practice}



\begin{quote}
Five words, and with them a first handful of Kannada letters read straight off the page. Let's gather only what you have already learned and make it feel easy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: Read them back}
Sound each out, left to right, before checking:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Read} & \textbf{Meaning} & \textbf{Native or borrowed} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}} \emph{namaskāra} & hello / greetings & Sanskrit \\
\textbf{\kn{ಧನ್ಯವಾದ}} \emph{dhanyavāda} & thank you & Sanskrit \\
\textbf{\kn{ಹೌದು}} \emph{haudu} & yes & native \\
\textbf{\kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}} \emph{illa} & no / there isn't & native (= Tamil \emph{illai}) \\
\textbf{\kn{ಸರಿ}} \emph{sari} & okay / correct & native (= Tamil \emph{sari}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The letters that did it: consonants carry a built-in \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}}; a \textbf{vowel sign} swaps that vowel (\kn{ಾ} for \textquotedblleft{}ā,\textquotedblright{} \kn{ಿ} for \textquotedblleft{}i,\textquotedblright{} \kn{ು} for \textquotedblleft{}u,\textquotedblright{} \kn{ೌ} for \textquotedblleft{}au\textquotedblright{}); a \textbf{virama} strips the vowel so a consonant can \textbf{stack under} the next as a conjunct (\emph{ottakṣara} — \kn{ಸ್ಕ}, \kn{ನ್ಯ}, \kn{ಲ್ಲ}); and a word-initial vowel gets a \textbf{full letter} (\kn{ಇ}).

Notice the pattern already: the two \textbf{greeting/politeness} words are Sanskrit loans; the three \textbf{everyday grammar} words are native Dravidian — and two of them (\emph{illa}, \emph{sari}) are shared almost unchanged with Tamil.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: A promise for later}
Kannada has a warm departure exchange built around going and coming back. It belongs in the later chapter where you learn those actions one at a time. For now, repeating the greeting is enough when you part.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all five — namaskāra · dhanyavāda · haudu · illa · sari
  \item greet and thank — \textquotedblleft{}namaskāra!\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}dhanyavāda.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read all five words aloud. Which two are Sanskrit loans, and which three are native Dravidian? (Loans: \emph{namaskāra}, \emph{dhanyavāda}. Native: \emph{haudu}, \emph{illa}, \emph{sari}.) Which one means \textquotedblleft{}okay / correct\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{sari}.)
